thread.title: ASIA MARKETS: Asian Markets Mostly Rise On Brighter Economic Data

author: morningstar.com
title: ASIA MARKETS: Asian Markets Mostly Rise On Brighter Economic Data
text:
By Gregor Stuart Hunter
Nikkei up 1.2% after 6 days of declines; stocks in China sink
Some Asian stock markets rebounded after the broad pullback that started the week, but Chinese equities weakened again following another muted manufacturing reading, weighing on Hong Kong stocks.
A gauge of manufacturing activity that some watch more closely than the official reading out Wednesday was flat for January and only modestly in expansion territory. That there was no change from December hinted that demand is weaker, said Julian Evans-Pritchard at Capital Economics.
The Shanghai Composite reversed modest early gains to end morning trading down 1.1%, while the Shenzhen Composite , home to smaller companies in China, fell a further 2.4% to hit levels last seen in mid-July.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng entered the midday break down 0.4% after rising as much as 0.5% early on, while the city's H-share index of Chinese-based firms also listed in the city finished the morning off 0.2% after climbing as much as 1.4% early on.
The China reading was in contrast to manufacturing PMI improving in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand for January. Meanwhile, Korean exports -- viewed as a proxy for the strength of global trade -- also rose last month by more than expected.
Japan's Nikkei Stock Average led the region with a 1.3% gain in the morning session after six straight declines.
The index was helped as banks rallied on strong financial results and the broader market got a lift from a lower yen. The U.S. dollar was recently around Yen109.34 versus Yen108.70 when Tokyo equities stopped trading Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Fujifilm (4901.TO) rebounded 13% to more than reverse yesterday's 8.3% drop following confirmation it would buy a controlling stake in Xerox Corp. (XRX) .
Taiwan stocks were also rebounding Thursday ahead of quarterly results from Apple. Weak demand for the company's iPhone X has weighed on the island's market. Taiwan is home to many Apple (AAPL) suppliers.
Market expectations had been too high for Apple's latest flagship iPhone X, and any sign of change on pricing would be closely watched, said Philip Li, senior portfolio manager at Value Partners. He added recently, "Bargaining power has been lying with the component suppliers."
The Taiex rose 0.7%, as did Australia's stock benchmark. The underperforming S&P/ASX 200, among the few major indexes globally to post a January decline, benefited Thursday from rebounding commodity prices. Oil futures were steady in Asian trading after overnight gains.
New Zealand's NZX 50 was recently down 0.6%, erasing the 55-point end-of-session jump Wednesday that enabled the index to notch a 13th-straight monthly gain.
Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve kept interest rates on hold as expected Wednesday. But language in its policy statement was changed to reflect confidence that inflation would stabilize around the central bank's 2% target, said Marvin Loh, a senior global market strategist at BNY Mellon.
"We view this change as an indication that the FOMC feels better about the current inflation outlook despite data that has not yet reflected much price or wage growth," he added, referring to the Federal Open Market Committee. Many market participants expect the Fed to next raise rates in March.
